dataset.title: Jornada Basin LTER (2018-2019) data and code for the Ecology publication “Shrub and grass soil-resource partitioning as modulated by precipitation amount and size of individual"

abstract.para: This data package contains data and code associated with a plant root tracer experiment (Study 469) conducted at the Jornada Basin LTER site in southern New Mexico, U.S.A, associated with the Ecology journal article “Shrub and grass soil-resource partitioning as modulated by precipitation amount and size of individual". The study was designed to investigate the root absorption profiles of dominant Prosopis glandulosa shrub and Bouteloua eriopoda grass. In September 2018 and September 2019, either LiCl tracer (treatment) or water (control) was injected to beneath 64 Prosopis glandulosa shrubs with co-located Bouteloua eripoda grasses. Injection depths ranged from 10 to 120 cm beneath the soil surface. Aboveground photosynthetic plant tissue was collected from target shrubs and grasses 21 days following each injection. Milled plant tissue samples were analyzed for Li content (concentration in ppm) using ICP-OES techniques in order to quantify plant root uptake activity. R scripts included in this package duplicate the data preparation and statistical analyses performed to model the soil-resource uptake of shrubs and grasses under divergent soil moisture conditions. This study and the dataset are completed.

Study Site Description and Environmental Variables

This study was conducted within the Jornada Basin LTER site, located north of Las Cruces, NM, USA (32.56°N, 106.78°W). The site receives a mean annual precipitation of 232 mm predominantly from summer monsoonal storms. Dominant vegetation species are Bouteloua eriopoda (black grama), a perennial C4 grass, and Prosopis glandulosa (honey mesquite), a perennial C3 shrub. Soil at the site is classified as Cacique loamy fine sand with weakly developed textural B (argillic) horizons overlaying semi-indurated to indurated caliche at ~30-60 cm in depth (Gile 1981; Monger 2006). The site has been protected from cattle grazing since 1996. Volumetric soil moisture data was collected from10 nearby neutron probes at the G-BASN NPP site located at the Jornada Basin LTER site (Virginia, Duniway, and Anderson 2025). Data was retrieved for the months of August, September, and October of 2018 and 2019 from depths of 30 cm, 60 cm, 90 cm, and 120 cm.

description.para: Experimental Design and Tracer Methodology
Experimental Design Overview:

We implemented a tracer experiment in 64 units of grass-shrub pairs, here referred to as experimental units, to address our questions regarding (i) the difference between plant species' uptake profiles, (ii) responses of uptake profiles to changes in soil moisture, and (iii) changes in shrub uptake profiles with aboveground plant growth.
Tracer Methodology:

We injected a Li tracer to a range of depths beneath the canopies of P. glandulosa shrubs that were surrounded by patches of B. eriopoda grass. We injected either a solution of 10 ml of 10% Sigma Aldrich LiCl solution (treatment) or 10 ml water (control) at each of 64 experimental units using a custom-built galvanized steel pipe injector. Each experimental unit consisted of one grass-shrub pair and received one injection at a single depth. The injector was flushed with water between treatments. Designated injection depths of 10, 50, 100, and 120 cm were randomly assigned within four groups of experimental units of similar shrub size, as described in the "grass-shrub pair selection" section below. In cases where caliche layers prevented injection to the target depth, injections were performed at the maximum achievable depth. Accordingly, samples were categorized by depths of 0-10 cm, 11-50 cm, 51-60 cm, 61-70cm, 71-80 cm, 81-100 cm. In order to assess potential differences in uptake profiles under different soil-moisture conditions, identical treatments were performed at each experimental unit in late September of 2018 and 2019. In order to address the impact of shrub size on uptake profiles, identical treatments were performed across experimental units representing shrubs of different aboveground volume (m^3; see "grass-shrub pair selection").
Grass-shrub Pair Selection:

We randomly selected experimental units (N = 64) at our study site which included a P. glandulosa shrub surrounded by B. eriopoda grass. Shrubs aboveground volume was estimated by measuring plant height and two perpendicular diameters, and ranged from 0.02 to 13.21 m^3. All grass patches were equal in size and distribution around target shrubs. We divided the 64 experimental units into four groups of 16 shrub-grass pairs according to mean shrub volume. To ensure a uniform distribution of injection depths across shrub sizes, we randomly assigned one of four injection treatment depths to every experimental unit within each size group. There were four replicate experimental units for each shrub size group and injection depth combination (for example, n = 4 "small" shrubs and their neighboring grasses received an injection at 10 cm depth). We randomly assigned one of each experimental unit per treatment depth and shrub size group to the control group (n = 16).
Sample Collection and Sample Analysis
Sample Collection:

21 days following injections, we harvested two grams of green leaves from P. glandulosa shrubs (n = 64) and black grama grasses (n = 64) from each experimental unit and stored samples in paper and plastic bags inside a cooler with ice. Samples were transported to Jornada Basin LTER headquarters and dried at 60⁰C for 72 hours prior to transport to Arizona State University for final preparation and analysis.
Sample Analysis:

Samples were analyzed for Li concentration (ppm) using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES). Samples were milled into a fine powder using an Across International VQ-N High Energy Ball Mill and collected in sterile scintillation vials. Milled plant tissue (0.1 g) was transferred along with five ml concentrated HNO3 into Teflon beakers which were then sealed and placed on hot plates within a fume hood for eight hours to allow acid digestion. Beakers were then vented on hot plates until “near dryness” (approximately 4 hours) and transferred via a 2% HNO3 rinse into 15 ml tubes, filled to a total volume of 10 ml. Samples were then weighed and centrifuged at 4000 RPM for five minutes using an Allegra X-14 Benchtop Centrifuge. Five mL of centrifuged sample was transferred into clean 15 mL test tubes and run on an Agilent 5900 ICP-OES to measure plant tissue Li content (ppm).

description.para: Statistical Analysis and R Code Workflow
Primary Statistical Analysis:

To construct root absorption profiles, we calculated the cumulative fraction of total measured Li across all samples within species groups for each sampling period. Following the Jackson et al. (1996), we applied the following model (modified from Gale and Grigal (1987)):
Y=1- β^d (Equation 1)

where Y = cumulative Li absorption fraction, d = soil depth, and β = fitted extinction coefficient. Estimated β values reflect the proportion of uptake with depth; lower values indicate greater proportions of uptake from shallow soil and higher values indicate deeper uptake.

To compare shrub and grass uptake profiles, we applied Equation 1 to data from both sampling periods to construct a single profile per species. To compare uptake profiles across soil-moisture conditions, we applied Equation 1 separately to data within each species and sampling period. Nonlinear least squares models were fit using the nls function in the stats package in R version 4.3.2 (Team 2023). 95% confidence intervals for estimates of β were calculated using the confint function in the stats package in R. We compared volumetric soil-water content between years at each depth category using a series of pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

To compare uptake profiles across mesquite shrub sizes, we used the sliding window technique with overlap (window size of n = 42) to identify 26 groups of observations ordered by aboveground shrub volume (m^3). Each group represents the full range of injection depths. We applied Equation 1 to calculate a β extinction coefficient for each shrub size group. Using the nls function in R, we fit the following Michaelis-Menten model (Ritz, Kniss, and Streibig 2015):
Y=(dx)/(x+e) (Equation 2)
where Y = β coefficient, d = upper limit of Y, x = mean shrub volume (m^3), and e = the value of x for which Y is halfway between zero and d.
Alternative/Secondary Statistical Analysis:
For each species, we calculated proportionate uptake by dividing the Li concentration (ppm) of each sample by the sum of all concentration measurements collected within the same sampling year.

We compared the 2-year median proportion of total Li tracer uptake of shrubs and grasses from each sample depth, by performing a series of Wilcoxon rank-sum tests using the rstatix package in R version 4.3.2.

To compared Li uptake across soil moisture conditions, we calculated the median proportion of total Li uptake observed during dry (2018) and wet (2019) years at each sample depth. We performed a series of Wilcoxon rank-sum tests using the rstatix package in R version 4.3.2.
R Code Workflow:

All scripts are written such that their associated working directory is a folder containing 3 subfolders with the names "Data," "Scripts," and "Figures." The workflow is separated into numbered scripts which prepare the raw data for analysis, perform statistical analysis, and produce corresponding figures. Scripts numbering (in filenames) reflects the order of operations performed in our analyses.

abstract.para: The Jornada Basin Long-Term Ecological Research (LTER) program is part of a national network of long-term ecological research sites funded by the US National Science Foundation (NSF). The Jornada LTER program has been continuously funded since 1982 to develop general principles governing changes between grassland and shrubland ecosystems based on long-term data collected in the Chihuahuan Desert. We translate our findings to dryland ecosystems around the world, and forecast the dynamics of future ecosystem states in response to changing climate and land use.
